title: London Concours 2026
excerpt: A pocket of automotive theatre hidden in the heart of the City.

sections.heading: Hidden in Plain Sight
sections.text:
London Concours begins with a contradiction.

You arrive surrounded by the City: buildings rising around you, traffic nearby and the unmistakable feeling of being in central London. Then you step through the gates of the Honourable Artillery Company and almost immediately, all of it seems to disappear.

The lawns open up in front of you, filled with cars, displays and collections, while the buildings remain visible beyond the trees like a reminder of where you actually are.

That contrast was probably our first real impression of the event.

A yellow supercar greeted visitors near the entrance before the grounds gradually opened into very different areas: private collections, hypercars, historic machinery, rally cars and carefully curated concours classes spread across the grass.

For its tenth anniversary, London Concours brought nine main classes to the HAC, ranging from Group A rally cars and American muscle to Porsche Sonderwunsch, tuners, dream cars and modern hypercars.

But standing there, the categories mattered less than the simple feeling of discovering what was hidden behind the walls.

The city was still there.

It just no longer felt like part of the afternoon.

sections.heading: Four Seasons in an Afternoon
sections.text:
The weather made sure the scene never stayed the same for very long.

Rain would fall heavily enough to send people looking for shelter, only for a break in the clouds to suddenly flood the lawns with sunlight. Then, minutes later, the grey returned.

From a photographer's perspective, it gave the event an atmosphere that a completely clear summer afternoon probably could not have produced.

Dark clouds gave the cars a heavier presence. Wet paint and bodywork began reflecting the surroundings differently. Water gathered across surfaces and the grass became deeper in colour, while the next ray of sunlight could completely transform the same scene again.

London Concours never settled into one visual identity that afternoon.

And somehow, that suited the setting.

The speakers, music and occasional exhaust note remained trapped inside the grounds while the towers of the City framed everything from outside. Despite being surrounded by one of Europe's busiest financial districts, we could barely hear it.

For a few hours, the HAC felt almost self-contained.

sections.heading: The Hypercar Lawn
sections.text:
If there was one area that repeatedly pulled us back, it was the Hypercars display.

The 2026 field was unusually concentrated: Bugatti Veyron, Lamborghini Reventón, Koenigsegg Agera N and Jesko, McLaren P1, Porsche 918 Spyder, Ferrari Monza SP2, Aston Martin Valkyrie and Valhalla, Gordon Murray T.50, Lamborghini Sián and Mercedes-AMG ONE all occupied the same lawn.

The AMG ONE was perhaps the clearest example of the kind of engineering represented there.

Its importance is easy to lose when surrounded by so many other hypercars, but the concept remains extraordinary: a road-legal car built around a Formula 1-derived 1.6-litre turbocharged V6, working with four electric motors for a combined 1,063 hp.

Seeing one statically is almost strange because so much of its identity revolves around what lies underneath the bodywork.

Beside machines like the Valkyrie, T.50 and P1, it also showed just how differently manufacturers have interpreted the same basic idea of the modern hypercar.

Different engines.

Different philosophies.

Different eras.

All occupying the same patch of London grass.

sections.heading: Familiar Shapes, Different Stories
sections.text:
Some cars stood out not because we had never seen the model before, but because the particular example gave us a reason to look again.

The Porsche 918 Spyder in Martini Racing design was one of them. The livery is not simply an aftermarket reference to Porsche's racing history. Martini Racing graphics were offered by Porsche for the 918 itself, reviving the colours associated with some of the marque's most recognisable competition cars. The 918 had already become part of Porsche history in its own right when it became the first road-legal production car to lap the Nürburgring Nordschleife in under seven minutes.

Another was the Aston Martin Vantage AMR in Halo Pack specification.

Its Stirling Green and Lime Green combination was directly inspired by Aston Martin Racing's #95 Vantage GTE, which won its class in the 2016 FIA World Endurance Championship. What initially looks like a particularly striking colour scheme therefore carries a direct connection to Aston Martin's contemporary racing programme.

But perhaps the most personal piece of provenance came from the 2019 McLaren Senna presented by EMM London.

Finished in Onyx Black, this particular car had belonged to Lando Norris, joining his personal collection in 2023 before EMM London handled its sale to the current owner in 2025. To mark the handover, and Norris’ Formula 1 World Championship, he signed the car in gold, changing his usual #4 to #1.

That small signature changes the car completely.

A Senna is already rare, with production limited to 500 examples. But provenance like this gives one particular chassis an identity that cannot simply be recreated with another specification or colour combination.

And that was one of the pleasures of London Concours.

You could recognise a car from twenty metres away, walk closer, and discover that the interesting part was not necessarily the model itself, but which example it was, who had owned it, or why that particular specification existed.

sections.heading: New Names Among Established Ones
sections.text:
Not everything on the lawn came with decades of history behind it.

The Elektron Quasar was perhaps the clearest example.

London Concours 2026 marked the Quasar's first public unveiling, placing a very new name among brands whose reputations were already firmly established. Elektron describes the all-electric hypercar as producing 2,413 hp, with four independent motors and production intended to be limited to 99 examples.

Whether it will eventually earn a place beside the established hypercars surrounding it is something only time can answer.

But seeing it there was part of the appeal.

London Concours was not only presenting cars whose importance had already been decided. It was also giving visitors the chance to encounter something at the beginning of its story.

The same contrast appeared across the event: decades-old rally machinery beside new hypercars, restored icons beside radical reinterpretations, familiar manufacturers beside names many visitors were probably seeing for the first time.

The lawn felt less like a timeline and more like different periods of automotive culture colliding in the same place.

sections.heading: Exclusive, Without Feeling Closed
sections.text:
Despite the machinery on display, London Concours did not feel socially intimidating.

There were no elaborate dress codes shaping the crowd in the way Chantilly's Garden Party did, nor the close-knit, almost family-like atmosphere we had experienced at Hasselt.

Here, the attention stayed much more firmly on the cars.

People gathered around displays, moved between collections, waited for gaps in the crowds and tried to get closer to whatever had caught their eye.

And it was crowded.

At times, getting a clean photograph meant waiting rather than simply finding another angle.

Yet that density also said something about the event. Cars of this calibre were being displayed inside one of London's most unusual private spaces, but access to the experience itself remained surprisingly straightforward.

It was exclusive in content rather than attitude.

Perhaps that is the trade-off that defines London Concours best.

Less lifestyle theatre.

Less focus on who is attending.

More emphasis on what has been assembled in front of you.

sections.heading: The Grand Depart
sections.text:
Then, towards the end of the afternoon, the event changed again.

Cars that had sat motionless across the lawns for hours began to wake up.

Doors opened.

Engines turned over.

People gathered around the exit.

One by one, the displays stopped being displays.

Thursday's traditional Grand Depart marked the end of the three-day event, sending the concours cars back out of the Honourable Artillery Company and into London.

After spending the afternoon seeing them arranged almost perfectly across the grass, watching them leave felt strangely different.

A parked hypercar can appear almost unreal.

Then the engine starts, the wheels turn and it suddenly becomes a car again.

The rain, the grey sky and the surrounding City only made the departure more theatrical. Machines that had spent the day hidden inside this small automotive world began disappearing one after another through the gates and back into London.

For a few hours, the HAC had managed to keep the city outside.

Then the cars woke up and returned to it.
